bituriges-cubi.t: Powerful Gallic people of Berry whose capital Avaricum, modern Bourges, was stormed by Caesar in one of the bloodiest sieges of the Gallic War.
bituriges-cubi.o: The Bituriges, whose name means 'kings of the world', occupied the middle Loire and Cher basins around Avaricum (Bourges). Livy tells a legend that in the 6th century BCE their king Ambigatus held supremacy over the Celts and sent his nephews Bellovesus and Segovesus to lead migrations into Italy and the Hercynian Forest. A related branch, the Bituriges Vivisci, later settled at Bordeaux.
bituriges-cubi.r: Their land was rich in iron ore, and the Bituriges were renowned smiths and metalworkers. Avaricum, defended by a massive timber-laced murus gallicus rampart, was one of the largest and wealthiest oppida in Gaul.
bituriges-cubi.e: In 52 BCE they joined Vercingetorix and burned some twenty of their own towns to starve the Romans, but spared Avaricum, which Caesar took after a hard siege, killing most of its inhabitants. Under Rome their territory became a civitas of Aquitania, the origin of the province of Berry.

bituriges-vivisci.t: Offshoot of the Bituriges settled on the Gironde estuary, whose trading port of Burdigala grew into Bordeaux.
bituriges-vivisci.o: Strabo notes that the Bituriges Vivisci were the only Celtic people living among the Aquitani, which suggests they migrated from the Bituriges Cubi of Berry to the lower Garonne, perhaps in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. Their emporium Burdigala stood on a bend of the Garonne.
bituriges-vivisci.r: Burdigala was a trading port linking the Atlantic with the Mediterranean by the Garonne and Aude route, handling tin, metals and Italian wine. Caesar does not name them, perhaps because they did not resist him.
bituriges-vivisci.e: Under Rome Burdigala became the capital of Aquitania and a rich city whose vineyards, based on a vine named Biturica after the people, laid the foundations of the Bordeaux wine trade. The poet Ausonius was born there in the 4th century.

baiocasses.t: Gallic people of the Bessin in Normandy whose town Augustodurum grew into Bayeux.
baiocasses.o: Known from Pliny and later Roman sources, the Baiocasses lived along the Calvados coast west of the Orne. In Caesar's day they were probably counted among the Armorican peoples.
baiocasses.r: No rulers or pre-Roman institutions are recorded.
baiocasses.e: Under Rome their chief town was Augustodurum, renamed Baiocasses in late antiquity, the origin of Bayeux. It became a bishopric, and in the 11th century the Bayeux Tapestry was made for its cathedral.

belgae-britain.t: Central southern British people around Winchester, whose name recalls the Belgae of northern Gaul and who formed a civitas of Roman Britain.
belgae-britain.o: Caesar wrote that the coastal parts of Britain had been settled by Belgae from Gaul who kept their tribal names, and Belgic coins circulated widely in the south from the 2nd century BCE. A people called Belgae is named only from Roman times, however, and their pre-conquest identity is uncertain; Winchester, the later Venta Belgarum, had a late Iron Age enclosure at Oram's Arbour.
belgae-britain.r: Before the conquest the region of Hampshire and Wiltshire seems to have fallen within the sphere of the Atrebates (Britain) and their kings Commius, Tincomarus and Verica, sharing their coinage and links with Gaul. Farming was rich on the chalk downs, and hillforts such as Danebury had been major storage centres in earlier centuries.
belgae-britain.e: After 43 the area may first have been part of the realm of Togidubnus in the Kingdom of the Regni. On his death it was organised as the civitas of the Belgae, with Venta Belgarum as its capital; Ptolemy also lists Aquae Sulis, Bath, among their towns. Winchester later became the royal seat of Wessex.

bellovaci.t: The most powerful of the Belgic peoples, around Beauvais, who fought Caesar in 57 BCE and led one of the last Gallic revolts in 51 BCE.
bellovaci.o: The Bellovaci lived in the modern Oise and Picardy around Beauvais. Caesar was told that they could field a hundred thousand men and had promised sixty thousand to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
bellovaci.r: Their society was led by a warrior nobility, and they had ties to the Aedui. Large sanctuaries such as Gournay-sur-Aronde, with displays of weapons and sacrificed animals, show their religious practice.
bellovaci.e: In 57 BCE they surrendered at Bratuspantium after the Aeduan Diviciacus spoke for them. In 51 BCE they rose under Correus, who died fighting. Under Rome their chief town became Caesaromagus, later Beauvais.

berones.t: A Celtic people of the upper Ebro in La Rioja, whose towns Vareia, Tritium and Libia lay on the routes into the Meseta.
berones.o: The Berones lived in the upper Ebro valley, in modern La Rioja, from about the 4th century BCE. Strabo described them as Celts, and their neighbours were the Autrigones, Pellendones and Vascones.
berones.r: Little is known of their government. Their towns included Vareia near Logroño, Tritium and Libia, and they lived from farming the fertile Ebro valley and herding. They reportedly served as mercenaries in conflicts of the 2nd century BCE.
berones.e: They came under Roman control in the 2nd century BCE during the Celtiberian wars. In 76 BCE Sertorius captured Vareia during his war against Rome. The Berones were absorbed into Hispania Citerior, and Tritium Magallum became a major Roman pottery centre.

balearic-islanders.t: The tower-building peoples of Mallorca and Menorca, whose stone talaiots and taulas still dot the islands and whose slingers fought for Carthage and Rome.
balearic-islanders.o: From around 1000 BCE the islanders of Mallorca and Menorca developed what archaeologists call the Talaiotic culture, named after the talaiots, massive dry-stone towers that dominated fortified villages. It grew out of the earlier Naviform culture of boat-shaped houses and stone tombs such as the Naveta des Tudons on Menorca.
balearic-islanders.r: There was no single state: the islands were divided among village communities, probably led by local chiefs, living from herding, farming and some trade with Phoenician and Punic merchants, especially from nearby Ebusus. Menorca's T-shaped taulas stood in sanctuary enclosures. The islanders were famed throughout the Mediterranean as slingers and served as mercenaries in Carthaginian armies, including Hannibal's.
balearic-islanders.e: Accused of sheltering pirates, the islands were conquered in 123 BCE by the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus, who took the name Balearicus and founded the towns of Palma and Pollentia. Talaiotic traditions faded under Roman rule, but hundreds of monuments survive.

bigerriones.t: Aquitanian people of the high Pyrenean valleys around Tarbes, who gave their name to Bigorre.
bigerriones.o: The Bigerriones lived in the upper Adour valley and the Pyrenean foothills of the modern Hautes-Pyrénées. Caesar lists them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
bigerriones.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Like other Aquitani they spoke a language related to Basque, and their economy combined mountain herding with farming in the valleys.
bigerriones.e: Under Rome their chief town was Turba, later Tarbes, within the province of Aquitania and then Novempopulana. Their name passed to the medieval County of Bigorre.

bergistani.t: A small Iberian people of the Catalan pre-Pyrenees whose repeated revolts against Cato in 195 BCE ended in their enslavement.
bergistani.o: The Bergistani lived in the upper Llobregat valley of central Catalonia, a region still called the Berguedà after them. They were an Iberian-speaking hill people whose main stronghold was the fortress of Bergium, perhaps near modern Berga.
bergistani.r: Little is known about their society beyond Livy's narrative. They lived from mixed farming and herding in a mountainous district and defended themselves from fortified hilltops.
bergistani.e: In 195 BCE they rose twice against the consul Cato. After the second revolt he took their strongholds and sold the inhabitants into slavery, and Bergium itself fell when its exiled leader helped the Romans inside. The territory was absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern Andalusia, in modern Granada, Almería and Jaén, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was Basti, near Baza, and they bordered the Oretani, Contestani and coastal Bastuli.
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and Basti, where the Lady of Baza, a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under Rome during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between Hispania Citerior and Baetica in Roman times.

barcid-iberia.t: The Carthaginian domain built in Iberia by Hamilcar Barca and his heirs, the silver-rich base from which Hannibal set out to invade Italy.
barcid-iberia.o: After losing Sicily in the First Punic War, Carthage sent Hamilcar Barca to Iberia in 237 BCE. Landing at Gadir, he conquered the Guadalquivir valley and its mines. After his death in about 229 BCE, his son-in-law Hasdrubal extended Carthaginian power by diplomacy and founded Qart Hadasht, later Carthago Nova, around 227 BCE.
barcid-iberia.r: Barcid Iberia was run almost as a family dominion of the Barcids, nominally under Carthage. Silver from mines near Qart Hadasht and the Sierra Morena paid for armies of Iberian, Celtiberian and African troops. Alliances with local rulers were sealed by marriages, such as Hannibal's to Himilce of Castulo. In 226 BCE the Ebro treaty with Rome fixed a northern limit.
barcid-iberia.e: Hannibal, in command from 221 BCE, took Saguntum in 219 BCE, starting the Second Punic War. Scipio captured Qart Hadasht in 209 BCE and won at Ilipa in 206 BCE, ending Carthaginian rule. The territory became the Roman provinces of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.

bosporan-kingdom.t: Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
bosporan-kingdom.o: Greek colonies on both sides of the Cimmerian Bosporus, such as Panticapaeum, Phanagoria and Theodosia, united under the Archaeanactid dynasty around 480 BCE. In 438 BCE power passed to Spartocus I, whose Spartocid descendants ruled for more than three centuries from Panticapaeum, modern Kerch, extending control over local Sindians and Maeotians.
bosporan-kingdom.r: The Spartocids called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples. Wealth came from grain, fish and slaves shipped to the Aegean: Leucon I (389-349 BCE) granted Athens tax-free grain purchases and was honoured there. Rich kurgan burials show a blend of Greek and Scythian and Sarmatian culture.
bosporan-kingdom.e: Under pressure from the Scythians, Paerisades V handed the kingdom to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 108 BCE. Later kings, such as Aspurgus and his successors, ruled as clients of Rome. The kingdom declined in the 3rd century CE and was overrun by the Huns in the 370s.
bosporan-kingdom.re: Ancient Greek religion, later also Christianity and Judaism

bibroci.t: British people named only once by Julius Caesar, among the groups that surrendered to him during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
bibroci.o: Known only from Caesar's Gallic War, the Bibroci were one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Cassi, who sent envoys to surrender to him in 54 BCE after the Trinovantes had come under his protection.
bibroci.r: Nothing is recorded of their government, rulers or way of life. Their territory is unknown; scholars have suggested places in the Thames valley or in Berkshire and Sussex, but no inscription or coin securely names them.
bibroci.e: They vanish from the record after Caesar's account. Their land was presumably absorbed by larger neighbours such as the Atrebates (Britain) or the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

belegezites.t: Slavic tribe settled in Thessaly in the 7th century, remembered for trading grain with besieged Thessalonica.
belegezites.o: The Belegezites were one of the Slavic groups that settled in the Balkans during the great migrations of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They occupied lands in Thessaly around Phthiotic Thebes and Demetrias on the Gulf of Volos. Almost everything known about them comes from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, a Byzantine collection of stories about Thessalonica.
belegezites.r: They lived as farming communities under their own chiefs, partly independent of Byzantium. During the Slavic siege of Thessalonica in the 670s they did not join the attackers but sold grain to the starving city, a sign of their prosperity and pragmatic relations with the Byzantines. Their name survives in later Byzantine sources as the region of Velegezitia.
belegezites.e: Over the 8th and 9th centuries Byzantium reasserted control over Greece through the theme system, and the Belegezites were gradually brought under imperial administration, converted to Christianity and absorbed into the Greek-speaking population. They leave few traces apart from place names.
belegezites.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

brigantes-ireland.t: People of south-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, bearing the same name as the great Brigantes confederation of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 lists the Brigantes in south-eastern Ireland, usually placed in the area of modern Wexford and Waterford, near the Coriondi and the Usdiae. The name, meaning roughly 'the high ones' or linked to the goddess Brigantia, is the same as that of the Brigantes of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. The shared name has encouraged theories of migration from Britain to Ireland, or of a common cult of a goddess later remembered as Brigit, but there is no evidence beyond the name. The south-east coast faced Wales and Gaul and was open to sea trade.
brigantes-ireland.e: The Irish Brigantes vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Leinster, the Kingdom of Osraige and the lands of the Deisi Muman.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the Jalón and Huerva valleys of modern Zaragoza province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included Segeda and Contrebia Belaisca, the modern Botorrita.
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The Botorrita bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from Contrebia Belaisca and record local regulations, while a Latin bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE Segeda enlarged its walls, which Rome treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by Carus of Segeda, the Celtiberians defeated the consul Nobilior, but after Numantia fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of Boeotia shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE Thebes was gathering them into a federation, an effort Plataea resisted by allying with Athens. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of Athens at Coronea in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia describes its 5th-century constitution: Boeotia was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with Thebes holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The King's Peace dissolved it in 386 BCE, but Pelopidas and Epaminondas revived it after 379 BCE and defeated Sparta at Leuctra. Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until Rome dissolved it in 171 BCE.

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the Pennines and northern England, from the Mersey and Humber to the Tyne. Their name is linked to the goddess Brigantia. By the time of the Roman invasion of 43 they were under the rule of Queen Cartimandua, who made a treaty with Rome and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. Cartimandua handed the fugitive Caratacus to the Romans in 51, and later her divorce from her consort Venutius split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 Venutius drove Cartimandua out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. Petillius Cerialis then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at York. The southern territory became a civitas centred on Isurium Brigantum, Aldborough, in Roman Britain.

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of Iberia, roughly from the Strait of Gibraltar to Almería, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as Malaka, Sexi and Abdera.
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under Hispania Ulterior and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into Baetica.
